text: A router moves packets between different networks using a routing table — a list of known destination networks and which next hop to send traffic toward. When multiple entries could match, the router picks the most specific one: a /32 host route beats a /24 subnet route, which beats the catch-all default /0 route.

Every device is configured with a default gateway — the router it hands traffic to whenever the destination isn't on its own local subnet. That's exactly why checking whether a device can ping its default gateway is such a common first troubleshooting step — it isolates the local segment from everything further upstream.

A static route is manually configured and doesn't adapt if a link goes down. Dynamic routing protocols let routers automatically learn networks and recalculate paths — Interior Gateway Protocols like OSPF work within one organization, while Exterior Gateway Protocols, namely BGP, exchange routes between separate autonomous systems across the public internet.

You won't be asked to configure OSPF or BGP in this course, but recognizing these names and what tier of network each operates at is expected baseline knowledge — a BGP route leak or hijack is a real, documented category of internet-scale security incident.
Next lesson: NAT, DHCP, and DNS in practice — the three services that quietly make every device's connection to the internet actually work, and what each one looks like when it breaks.
